description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: Good Is the Enemy of Great
cards.subtitle: Your quarterly earnings hit target three years straight. Nobody's asking why you should change.
body: The revenue is decent. The board is satisfied. There's no crisis to solve, no fire to put out. So the strategy meeting ends with minor tweaks.
Good results erase urgency. The distance from failure to good is shorter than good to great.
cards.takeaway: Comfortable performance is the biggest barrier to exceptional performance.

cards.title: Level 5 Leaders Are Quiet, Not Charismatic
cards.subtitle: You expected to find the bold CEO on magazine covers. You found him at the failing company instead.
body: The best-performing companies had leaders nobody had heard of. They sat in meetings and said less.

• When things went right, they credited the team
• When things failed, they looked inward first
• Celebrity status correlated with mediocre results
cards.takeaway: Quiet resolve outperformed loud vision.

cards.title: Get the Right People Before the Right Strategy
cards.subtitle: You spent six months perfecting the strategy deck. The wrong team executed it anyway.
body: Markets shift. Competitors copy. Technology changes. But a team that thinks clearly can pivot when needed.
The right people don't need motivating. Strategy matters less when you have to explain it constantly.
cards.takeaway: Who comes before what.

cards.title: Confront the Brutal Facts, Keep the Faith
cards.subtitle: The optimists kept saying 'we'll be rescued by Christmas.' They didn't make it to spring.
body: Stockdale survived eight years as a POW. He never denied how bad things were. But he never stopped believing he'd get out.
The ones who died first were the cheerful ones—the ones who kept setting hopeful deadlines that passed.
cards.takeaway: Denial and faith are opposites, not partners.

cards.title: The Hedgehog Knows One Thing Well
cards.subtitle: You're chasing twelve opportunities. Your competitor owns one thing completely.
body: Three circles: what you're best at, what makes you money, what you care about. Most companies operate in two circles.
Great ones found the center where all three overlap and stayed there.
cards.takeaway: You can't be best in the world at everything.

cards.title: The Flywheel Has No Single Defining Push
cards.subtitle: The journalist asks which decision turned it around. You can't point to one.
body: Push a massive flywheel once. Nothing. Push again. Still nothing. Keep pushing. Eventually it turns. Then faster.

• No single push did it
• The tenth push worked because of the first nine
• Momentum looks inevitable only after it arrives
cards.takeaway: Outsiders want the breakthrough moment. Insiders remember years of repetition.

cards.title: Discipline Replaces Bureaucracy
cards.subtitle: The more policies in the handbook, the more people who can't be trusted.
body: Bureaucracy exists because someone made a bad decision once. Then someone wrote a rule. Then the rule required approval.
Disciplined people don't need oversight. The companies with the thinnest handbooks moved fastest.
cards.takeaway: Hire discipline and you won't need to legislate it.

cards.title: Technology Is an Accelerator, Not a Creator
cards.subtitle: You bought the software before you figured out what problem it solves.
body: The failing companies chased technology trends first. ERP systems, data warehouses, websites—adopted because competitors had them.
The great companies knew what they needed to do, then found tech to do it faster.
cards.takeaway: Pioneers in tech application, not tech adoption.

cards.title: Stop Doing Lists Matter More
cards.subtitle: That project is profitable. It still doesn't fit. You keep it anyway.
body: Everyone builds to-do lists. Great companies kept stop-doing lists. They killed projects that made money but blurred focus.
Saying no to profitable work is harder than saying yes. Diversification is often just scattered attention.
cards.takeaway: Busy calendars hide the lack of direction.

cards.title: The Comparison Companies Had the Same Chances
cards.subtitle: Same industry. Same decade. Same starting resources. One succeeded. One blamed circumstances.
body: Every great company in the study was paired with a direct competitor. Same market, same resources, same regulatory environment.
One made disciplined choices. The other made excuses.
cards.takeaway: Luck doesn't explain pairs in identical conditions.

cards.title: Culture Eats Everything
cards.subtitle: The founder retires. Half the executives leave with him. Revenue drops 40% in a year.
body: Great companies kept running when the CEO left. Comparison companies collapsed.

• The difference wasn't the leader's skill
• It was whether they built systems or cults of personality
• What happens when you leave the room is the real test
cards.takeaway: Culture-driven companies survive succession.

cards.title: Big Goals Need a Hedgehog Foundation
cards.subtitle: The vision statement promises to transform the industry. You're not even good at the core business yet.
body: Big goals work when rooted in deep competence. Set a massive target in what you're best at—catalytic. Set it in something you're mediocre at—catastrophic.
Both types of companies had big goals. One group knew where to aim.
cards.takeaway: Audacity inside competence compounds. Audacity outside competence destroys.

cards.title: Acquisitions Rarely Drive Greatness
cards.subtitle: You bought three companies this year to fill strategic gaps. All three are underperforming.
body: Comparison companies acquired their way toward greatness—buying capabilities they lacked, chasing growth through deals. It rarely worked.
Great companies acquired to accelerate momentum they already had, not to create it from scratch.
cards.takeaway: Buying capability doesn't transfer understanding.

cards.title: The Best Leaders Give Credit and Take Blame
cards.subtitle: Success? She credits the team. Failure? He blames the market. Guess which one led the great company.
body: When things went right, Level 5 leaders pointed outward—team, timing, luck. When things failed, they looked inward.
Comparison company leaders reversed it. The consistency was strong enough to predict outcomes.
cards.takeaway: One pattern correlated with greatness. The opposite with mediocrity.

cards.title: Consistency Compounds Faster Than Intensity
cards.subtitle: Year one: all-hands transformation. Year two: restructuring. Year three: back to basics. Year four: new CEO.
body: Comparison companies swung between radical change and stagnation. Great companies repeated the same disciplined actions, year after year.
No drama. Just direction. Intensity burns out. Consistency accumulates.
cards.takeaway: Steady direction beats dramatic pivots.

cards.title: The Stockdale Paradox Is About Holding Two Truths
cards.subtitle: You need to believe you'll win and admit you're losing. Most people can only do one.
body: Faith that you'll prevail in the end. Honesty about how bad things are right now. Held simultaneously.

• Drop faith—you give up
• Drop honesty—you drift on delusion
• Optimism without facts is denial
cards.takeaway: The productive zone is holding both at once.

cards.title: Doom Loop Companies Lurch From Fad to Fad
cards.subtitle: New leader. New strategy. New org chart. Disappointing results. New leader.
body: Comparison companies followed a pattern: change direction, get disappointing results, panic, change direction again.
Each lurch reset whatever momentum existed. They never pushed long enough to break through.
cards.takeaway: Reaction kills accumulation. Every pivot restarts the clock.

cards.title: Greatness Is Not a Function of Size
cards.subtitle: The competitor has ten times your revenue and half your clarity. You're faster.
body: The study included companies of different sizes. Scale didn't predict greatness.
What mattered was clarity about what to do and consistency in doing it.
cards.takeaway: Small and focused beats large and scattered.

cards.title: Results Speak Louder Than Charisma
cards.subtitle: He was on the cover of three magazines this year. His stock is down 30% since he started.
body: The most celebrated CEOs of that era led comparison companies—not the great ones. Media visibility predicted mediocre returns.
Obscurity correlated with sustained performance. Quiet leaders built better institutions.
cards.takeaway: The best story and the best company are rarely the same.

cards.title: Greatness Is a Choice, Not a Circumstance
cards.subtitle: Same market. Same decade. Same starting point. One blamed conditions. One chose differently.
body: Every pair faced the same industries, the same eras, the same conditions. The separation came from compounding choices.
The stage was identical. The script was chosen.
cards.takeaway: Circumstances don't determine outcomes—responses do.
